About this issue

This is where science-fiction comics begin. Fiction House was a pulp-magazine shop first, and Planet Comics was built as the four-color twin of its Planet Stories pulp: rocket men, ray guns, hostile worlds and square-jawed pilots, twelve years before the genre became respectable. Launched in January 1940 and packaged through the Eisner & Iger studio, it was the first American comic book devoted entirely to science fiction, and it stayed on newsstands for 73 issues.

Issue #1 introduces Flint Baker, the rocketeer whose Mars expedition sets the tone for everything the title would do: pace over plausibility, spectacle over science. Alongside him you get Auro, Lord of Jupiter, and a stack of one-shot features the studio was clearly using to find out what stuck. The drawing is rough in places, but the energy is real, and you can watch a genre invent its own visual grammar page by page.

Read it as a time capsule: the space-opera clichés later generations grew up on are being minted here, in public domain, sixty-plus pages at a time. If you only sample one Fiction House book, make it this one.

Source: Internet Archive — scan courtesy Internet Archive comics collection (c2c fan scan).
